sourceChecks.botany: Plants generally draw on daytime-stored starch at night; source https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.00669 (John Innes Centre/eLife 2013). Avoid claiming all species respond identically in a 24-hour pause.
sourceChecks.comparison: QuirkScience publisher film list checked Nov 11, with Nov10 'What If You Dug a Hole Through the Earth and Jumped In?' 1:03. This is a question→explained-consequence format observation, NOT evidence of its engagement, nor has the first 2s been watched.

proposedRevision.openingQuestion: Would every living thing struggle immediately if leaves stopped making new food?
proposedRevision.lastFrameAnswer: Same sapling still healthy at dawn; a labeled normal/paused comparison changes back to 'photosynthesis on', with no instant oxygen catastrophe.
truthfulHooks: What if every plant stopped making food today?
What if photosynthesis paused for one day?
What if the world's green engines paused?
What if leaves stopped using sunlight today?
proposedRevision.selectedHook: What if every plant stopped making food today?
proposedRevision.scriptEnglish: What if every plant stopped making food today? Leaves would pause their work of turning sunlight into sugar. But the oxygen in our sky wouldn't suddenly disappear. Many plants store starch for nights like these. Watch this tree: it stays green as the hours pass. When daylight returns tomorrow, the leaves can start making sugar again. One day wouldn't empty the sky. It shows how much life quietly depends on the next sunrise.
